https://www.itv.com/news/calendar/2025-0.title: Sheffield tree campaigner 'amazed' after council apology
https://www.itv.com/news/calendar/2025-0.text:
A council has admitted that that it "ignored, belittled and condemned" protesters trying to protect trees in an apology to one campaigner.
Isabel O'Leary was among a group of residents who attempted to disrupt the felling of trees in Sheffield during a bitter dispute which made international headlines.
Now, seven years after the end of the protests, she has had a letter from the city council's chief executive apologising for her treatment.
Kate Josephs admitted the council "got many things wrong" and made "significant mistakes and errors of judgment".
She said: “I am sorry for how we ignored, belittled and condemned the actions of the street tree campaigners such as yourself.”
Ms O'Leary said: "I am amazed that they signed it off, because they are admitting to a lot of things, so that's great."
The tree-felling programme was part of a 25-year £2.2billion private finance initiative agreement between the council and contractor Amey to resurface pothole-ridden road system and maintain roadside trees.
The company was tasked with cutting down and replacing 17,500 trees.
It led to long-running protests throughout 2016 and 2018 including daily confrontations between objectors and contractors in some of the city’s leafiest suburbs and several unwarranted arrests.
Ms O'Leary was among several protesters threatened with injunctions.
She says she was "forced" into signing a letter banning her from protesting.
"The threat was that you'd be taken to the high court with potentially ruinous damages against you," she said.
"To avoid being taken to court, I signed an undertaking to not do anything that would stop a tree being felled. So I wasn't allowed to stand under a tree on the highway.
"I also wasn't allowed to encourage other people to do anything to stop trees being felled."
In total more than 5,000 trees were removed. In an inquiry led by former United Nations official Sir Mark Lowcock published in 2023 Sheffield City Council was found to have been guilty of dishonesty and a lack of transparency.
In her letter, Ms Josephs said: “Those mistakes and errors of judgement resulted in a large number of healthy street trees being felled that should not have been. That, in itself, resulted in substantial environmental degradation and loss of habitat and amenity value, and should not have happened.
“We also closed our ears to those people who were warning us about the mistakes that we were about to make as an organisation and that, in so doing, we lost the trust and confidence of our communities.
“As you know, our ‘we know best’ attitude resulted in serious harm to the city’s environment, our reputation nationally and globally, the wellbeing of our staff, and for campaigners who were trying to persuade us to take a different path. For that we are truly sorry."
Ms O'Leary now wants other campaigners - including some who were given hefty fines - to receive similar apologies.
"There's people who got suspended prison sentences and they have had no exoneration. Their employment might be impacted as this is on their record," she said.
A Sheffield City Council spokesperson said: "The council is in the process of agreeing terms of the apologies and has issued a draft apology to all undertakers.
"We will not comment on individual apologies or actions taken.
"As a council we remain committed to delivering apologies to those impacted by its actions in the street trees dispute."

image.caption: The controversial tree-felling programme was part of a 25-year £2.2billion private finance initiative agreement between Sheffield council and contractor Amey to cut down and replace 17,500 trees.
An independent inquiry into the Sheffield tree-felling controversy has found that the council misled the public and the courts. Credit: PA Images

https://www.itv.com/news/2025-08-31/bade.title: Kemi Badenoch vows to "maximise" oil and gas extraction in the North Sea
https://www.itv.com/news/2025-08-31/bade.text:
Kemi Badenoch has committed the Tories to “maximise the extraction of our oil and gas” from the North Sea.
The Conservative Party leader said it was “absurd” to leave the fossil fuel resources untapped.
But the government said issuing new licences for oil and gas exploration would “not take a penny off bills” and would accelerate the “worsening climate crisis.”
Mrs Badenoch will use a speech in Aberdeen on Tuesday to set out her plans.
She is expected to announce that the Tories plan to completely overhaul the North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA), which oversees the issuing of licences, dropping the word transition and giving it a simple order to extract the maximum possible amount of fossil fuels.
A Conservative government would make “maximising extraction” its goal if it wins power, rather than measures aimed at shifting the North Sea industry away from fossil fuels.
As part of their plans, the Conservatives have pledged to "free the sector from unnecessary red tape," as well as renaming the NSTA the 'North Sea Authority."
The Conservatives say their new mandate will remove emission reduction through electrification requirements, restrictions on venting and flaring, and forcing producers to focus on green developments such as carbon storage technologies.
They say it would also free the sector from the strict net-zero requirements that are attached to the issuing of new offshore oil and gas licenses, whilst the same oil and gas is imported from overseas.
Ahead of her speech, Mrs Badenoch pledged that “we are going to get all our oil and gas out of the North Sea”.
She said: “We are in the absurd situation where our country is leaving vital resources untapped whilst neighbours like Norway extract them from the same seabed.
"With the ONS confirming that economic growth is down partly because of falling oil and gas extraction, we cannot afford not to be doing everything to get hydrocarbons out of the ground."
She went on to claim: “Britain has already decarbonised more than every other major economy since 1990, causing us to face some of the highest energy prices in the developed world. This is not sustainable, and it cannot continue.
Badenoch described Labour's net-zero policies as a "unilateral act of economic disarmament," as well as an "impossible ideology of net-zero by 2050."

Responding to the Conservative plans, a Department for Energy Security and Net Zero spokesman said: “We are already delivering a fair and orderly transition in the North Sea to drive growth and secure skilled jobs for future generations, with the biggest ever investment in offshore wind and three first-of-a-kind carbon capture and storage clusters.
“We are committed to delivering the manifesto commitment to not issue new licences to explore new fields because they will not take a penny off bills, cannot make us energy secure, and will only accelerate the worsening climate crisis.”
A Labour Party spokeswoman said: “We’ll take no lectures from Kemi Badenoch. Every family and business paid the price of the Conservatives’ failure to secure the UK’s energy.
“The Conservatives oversaw thousands of lost jobs in the North Sea. In contrast, this Labour government is investing in the North Sea’s clean energy future, creating good jobs in offshore wind, hydrogen and carbon capture and storage, as we take back control of our energy for good.”
Offshore Energies UK chief executive David Whitehouse said: “As long as the UK continues to use oil and gas, it makes sense to produce as much of it as we can here at home.
“Every barrel of oil and gas we leave in the North Sea is a barrel we’ll need to import.
“Even in a net zero future, the UK will use 10-15 billion barrels of oil and gas between now and 2050. Current plans show the UK will produce less than four billion barrels, leaving us increasingly reliant on imports.
“Producing it here supports jobs, strengthens our economy, and improves our energy security.”

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.
ITV Central's Lee Comley reports on the group of activists who smashed through security gates at Moog Aircraft Group's factory in Wolverhampton
Just before 4am, protesters slammed through security gates at Moog Aircraft Group’s factory on Valiant Way in Wolverhampton, before releasing a smoke flare, and then making their way on to the roof.
Each step was documented and shared on social media.
The four activists say they’re from a group called ‘Palestinian Martyrs for Justice’. They wore T-shirts of Palestinians who’ve been killed.
A surgeon named Adnan al-Bursch, who was 50. Hossam Shabat, a journalist aged 23. Academic Refaat Alareer, who was 44, and 17-year-old Raghd al-Jabri, who was killed with her mother and siblings.
The group was targeting the Moog factory because it claims that parts made there go into aircraft used by Israeli forces to train pilots to fly F-35 and F-16 fighter jets. These aircraft are said to be used to bomb targets in Gaza.
Later in the morning, police had made their way onto the roof and arrested those involved, with people in climbing gear making their way up to retrieve the protesters' tents and tools they’d used to break through skylights.
The factory was heavily secured during the morning, with a cordon in place around it until midday. I spoke to one local protester who’d come to support those who’d climbed the roof. Arif told me he was waving his Palestinian flag because "People can relate to this flag, they know what’s going on".
Police have arrested four people on suspicion of criminal damage offences, saying significant damage was caused to skylights and solar panels. By early afternoon, security had lessened, and the factory was back working again, just hours after the group had broken through the security gates.
We contacted Moog for comment on both the actions of the protesters and the claims made in their social media videos, but have not yet received a response.
We did, however, receive a response from the Government: "As set out to Parliament last September, we have suspended licences for exports of military equipment to the IDF that might be used in military operations in Gaza, based on our assessment that these could be used to commit or facilitate serious violations of International Humanitarian Law.
"We have not suspended all export licences for military equipment, as some are not for use by the IDF in Gaza, including items such as trainer aircraft and components for missile defence systems, and parts for military systems that are re-exported to other countries, including NATO allies."

https://www.itv.com/news/calendar/2025-0.title: 'Where do we put the stuff?' Rotherham residents frustrated over halt to paid brown bin service
https://www.itv.com/news/calendar/2025-0.text:
This is a modal window.
Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.
End of dialog window.
This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.
Video report by Vicki Smith.
Garden waste collections in Rotherham have been suspended with immediate effect until the end of August, amid a staff shortage.
The decision, announced by Rotherham Council, means households will not receive their usual brown bin collection service for the rest of the month.
Garden waste collections in the town are paid for with a subscription service, with residents paying out an annual fee of more than £40 to sign up.
Norman Anderson, a resident in Todwick, is concerned about the pause to bin collections, as his garden maintenance results in lots of waste.
"The question of course is 'Where do we put the stuff? How do we get rid of it?"
"My trees are starting to get ready for cutting, got the secateurs ready and I have nowhere to put the stuff. The bins full."
Norman is being supported by his local councillor Cllr Joshua Bacon who says he wasn't given any forewarning about this from the council.
"The bins full."
Cllr Bacon, who represents Aston & Todwick, said: "I have had lots of correspondence from rightly frustrated residents."
The council said it was prioritising general waste collections to ensure essential services continue.
In a statement, the authority said: "We understand this is frustrating and sincerely apologise for the inconvenience.
"Please be assured that we are actively recruiting new staff to bolster the service and making changes intended to make it more efficient and effective in the future."
Andrew Bramidge, Strategic Director Regeneration and Environment at Rotherham Council said: "We have got people starting this week and next week."
"Normally we recruit agency staff to backfill but this year for some reason there's been less agency staff around."
He added: "We are very sorry we've had to take this action but we have had to prioritise so that we can focus on the types of waste that are more problematic at this time of year."
Residents who have already placed their brown bins out for collection have been asked to return them from the kerbside.
Garden waste collections are expected to resume on Monday 1 September.
The council said it would issue another update by Friday 29 August if further delays occur.
The authority said it was "considering the best way to make amends" to subscribers for the disruption and would share further information in due course.

https://www.itv.com/news/central/2025-08.title: Anger over 'senseless' roadworks on major route, with roads closed and town left gridlocked
https://www.itv.com/news/central/2025-08.text:
Anger is growing at what’s been labelled a “totally senseless” roadworks project on the A38 through Worcestershire - with multiple road closures and diversions causing significant delays.
The £50 million Bromsgrove Route Enhancement Project, or BREP, aims to widen a key part of the route which acts as a bypass to the town centre. But as the works rumble on, traffic is being forced through the town itself.
“They say it’s a ‘major project’ - but realistically, it’s not,” said campaigner Jonathan Coleman.
“It's widening some junctions. It's adding some traffic control. It should be a job that should be done in six to 12 months.
“For it to go on as long as it has done, and how long it will do, is just unacceptable.”
Despite it being the school holidays, when traffic levels traditionally fall, residents say the town is gridlocked on a regular basis.
Gesturing towards the long line of cars inching their way past, he said that sight has now become the norm.
“This is pretty typical and regular. And we’re in school holidays, so this is no not as bad as it will be in a few weeks’ time,” he said.
“People take journeys which should take minutes, but can now take over an hour. It's beyond ridiculous.”
Someone who knows that pain only too well is Debbie Alexander.
She has to do a nursery run in the morning, with two drop-offs - a trip which, before the works began, took her around half an hour. Now though, she said, it often takes more than double that.
“I’m very angry - there’s no accountability,” she said.
“The whole place is just gridlocked.
“It is directly as a result of the works, but the work that’s being carried out - they keep telling us it’s going to help with local traffic.
“Nobody can actually see that, and nobody is convinced that that’s actually going to happen.”
She said she wants to see the council hold contractors to account over the works, and scale back those she said were “senseless”.
They include a new cycle route from the railway station. Instead of taking a direct route into the town centre, cyclists will be taken on a circuitous journey through two nearby estates - which have had their main access road sealed off for three months while the work takes place.
“Nobody will do that, they’ll just use the direct road - it’s nonsense,” she added.
“I just can’t get my head around that at all.”
In response, a spokesperson for Worcestershire County Council said: “This major investment will increase capacity along the A38 and improve walking and cycling facilities.
“We recognise and apologise for any inconvenience caused by these works. Every effort has been made to plan and coordinate the programme to minimise disruption, with schemes delivered concurrently where possible to shorten the overall duration and manage costs.
“The highway network in Bromsgrove faces continued pressure from housing and commercial growth, alongside essential maintenance, utility works, and local events. All works are carefully coordinated and measures such as lane restrictions or temporary one-way systems are used to avoid full closures wherever possible.”
The current works form part of Phase Three of the BREP project, and are due to finish at the end of 2026.
But there is a Phase Four to come, with no date yet set for that - meaning the misery for motorists is unlikely to end any time soon.

https://www.itv.com/news/central/2025-08.title: Midlands to be hit by strike disruption on CrossCountry trains over August bank holiday weekend
https://www.itv.com/news/central/2025-08.text:
Strike action over the August bank holiday will see no CrossCountry services at all running on Saturday 23 August, meaning no direct trains connecting Birmingham to Leicester, Derby or Nottingham.
The operator has advised people to avoid travelling over the bank holiday weekend, as RMT members including train managers and conductors go on strike.
CrossCountry said trains on Sunday 24 August may also be subject to cancellations, and a "very limited" service will run on Monday 25 August between 8am and 6pm.
All services are expected to be busy.
It said some managers are available to help provide a limited service on the Monday, but the bank holiday weekend has reduced the number of people able to work on the Saturday, meaning no services can run.
The operator said tickets on its trains valid for the bank holiday weekend could instead be used either on Thursday 21 August and Wednesday 27 August.

Passengers strongly advised not to travel

No service between Leicester, Cambridge and Stansted Airport.

https://www.itv.com/news/central/2025-08.text:

Video footage shows the moment the plane had to make an emergency landing on the runway (credit: Harley Killingsworth)
Birmingham Airport has reopened after a day of disruption following an 'incident with a light aircraft' on the runway.
“Following the aircraft incident today, the runway has reopened and operations have resumed,” the airport said in an update posted on X.
It apologised for the disruption caused by the incident and said passengers must check flight details and follow advice issued by their airlines.
The airport added: “Our teams have worked as quickly as possible, in line with strict protocols, which must be followed to ensure a safe reopening of the runway following a prolonged closure.”
West Midlands Police has confirmed that a small aircraft was involved in an emergency landing around 1:40pm.
Officers are among the emergency crews at the scene and one person has been reported to have minor injuries.
The Air Accidents Investigation Branch say they have started an investigation into the incident. They say a "multi-disciplinary team including inspectors with expertise in aircraft operations, engineering and recorded data have been deployed to the airport."
East Midlands Airport said in a statement that it has accepted three diverts from Birmingham Airport this afternoon due to Birmingham’s runway being temporarily closed.
They are unable to take any further diverts at this stage without affecting their operation.
It comes just a week after flights at airports across the UK - including Birmingham, Heathrow, Gatwick and Edinburgh - were grounded while a technical issue was being investigated.
A gear-up landing is when an aircraft lands without its landing gear being fully extended.
The aircraft is a Beech B200 Super King Air and was heading from Birmingham to Belfast, according to the map it looked like it had done multiple loops over the West Midlands before returning.
Arrivals have been diverted to other airports, including those from Paris, Skathios, Malaga, Mahon, Palma and Faro.
Departures were delayed until 7 pm include those to Istanbul, Antalya, Isle of Man, Bucharest and Rome.
The Civil Aviation Authority has been informed, and the airport has suspended operations as an investigation is carried out.
A spokesperson said: “In the event of delays or cancellations, passengers will be expected to be provided with food and drink as well as accommodation if delayed overnight.”
Three people were treated at the scene of an emergency landing at Birmingham Airport, West Midlands Ambulance Service (WMAS) said.
“We were called at 1.45pm to an incident involving a light aircraft at Birmingham Airport. Hazardous Area Response Team (HART) paramedics and three paramedic officers were sent to the scene,” WMAS said in a statement.
“Upon arrival we found three patients from the aircraft, all of whom were assessed and discharged at the scene.”
In a statement, Birmingham Airport has said: “Following an aircraft incident, the runway is temporarily closed.
“We apologise for the inconvenience this will cause.
“We will keep passengers already at the airport informed, and those due to travel later today are advised to check the status of their flight before coming to the airport.
“We will continue to issue updates when we can.”

Woodgate Aviation said one of its Beechcraft fixed-wing aircraft was involved in an emergency landing at Birmingham Airport on Wednesday.
It said in a statement: “The turbo-prop aircraft was on a flight to Belfast International Airport when it developed landing gear problems. The aircraft returned to Birmingham and made an emergency landing and the main under-carriage collapsed on touch down.
“Two crew members and a passenger were on board but were uninjured.
“The aircraft remains on the runway and Woodgate Aviation will be co-operating fully with Air Accident investigators and airport services.
“We would like to pay tribute to the professionalism of our colleagues and the emergency services at the airport for their prompt action.”
